slots.label: causal-overclaim
slots.description: If two variables are correlated, one must cause the other.
slots.repair: Association alone does not rule out reverse causation or third variables.
slots.repairQuestion: Name one alternative explanation for the exercise-stress correlation besides exercise causing lower stress.
slots.repairCriteria: Repaired when the learner gives reverse causation or a third-variable explanation.

slots.label: correlation-useless overcorrection
slots.description: Because correlation is not causation, a correlation tells us nothing useful.
slots.repair: Correlation can be valuable for prediction and for generating hypotheses, even when it does not prove cause.
slots.repairQuestion: What is one useful thing a correlation can do even if it does not prove causation?
slots.repairCriteria: Repaired when the learner mentions prediction, description, screening, or hypothesis generation.

slots.label: control-equals-proof
slots.description: Adding a few statistical controls automatically proves causation.
slots.repair: Controls help only for variables measured well and modeled appropriately; unmeasured confounding or design problems can remain.
slots.repairQuestion: Why might statistical controls improve but not automatically prove a causal claim?
slots.repairCriteria: Repaired when the learner says controls may miss unmeasured or poorly measured confounders or that design still matters.

slots.text: Correlation is evidence of association, not by itself proof of cause. Causal claims require ruling out plausible alternatives such as reverse causation and confounding through design, timing, controls, or converging evidence. Correlations are still useful for prediction and hypothesis generation.
